version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm: page_alloc: make defrag_mode retries follow the promoted order

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the behavior of page allocation in defrag_mode to make retries follow the promoted order, rather than the original request order. This change is intended to prevent indefinite retrying by requests that are not movable, which can lead to reclaim storms and excessive memory pressure. The patch treats promoted requests as costly orders, resetting progress counters for them and checking compaction results at the promoted order. It also resets retry counters when a fallback attempt is taken, allowing it to get a full retry budget before the OOM killer is considered. This change aims to improve performance and reduce memory pressure in systems with high inode churn under memory.low protection.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author agrees that the cleanup changes are redundant and will be folded into the original patch, indicating no further revision is needed.

The author is addressing Johannes Weiner's concern about the effectiveness of the promoted path in reducing reclaim storms. The author built a reproducer to test the patch and found that it significantly reduces reclaim storms, with no measurable difference between the two floors (priority floor and COMPACT_SUCCESS retry limit).

Author acknowledges that the extra SYNC_FULL passes do not provide benefits in this specific workload and agrees to remove them.

The author is addressing a concern about the behavior of defrag_mode in certain scenarios, specifically when I/O is removed and tmpfs is used. They mention that every exhausted order-0 refill does a whole-zone SYNC_FULL pass before falling back, which increases PSI and slows down churn. The author asks for a preference on how to handle this situation, indicating they don't have a strong opinion either way.
review_comments.raw_body:
Will fold it into the fix itself. The cleanup changes the same places as
the fix. It makes zero sense to keep it separate.

---

I built a reproducer around what we saw in production, which was oomd
killing the workload on sustained PSI, so PSI and the number of times
ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT gets dropped are the headline numbers. 32G VM, 8 CPUs:

 - fill memory with 4K anon pages in a cgroup, memory.low = fill + 1G,
   so page cache beyond that stays reclaimable;

 - pin one page in every pageblock with io_uring registered buffers[1],
   except one block in 50 (2%), so whole blocks can be made but only
   from a few places. Without the pins rc5 does not storm in 180s:
   compaction makes 130-210 blocks per run and every retry loop ends in
   one. The storm needs blocks to be hard to produce, and the pin
   fraction is the knob for that;

 - free one page in eight so ~4G sit scattered in movable blocks;

 - turn on defrag_mode and run 8 build-like workers on btrfs for 180s:
   write 1-64K files, read earlier ones back, unlink 20%, fdatasync
   every 50 creates.

Kernels: v7.3-rc5; the fix as posted; the fix with the priority floor
and the COMPACT_SUCCESS retry limit on the requested order. Three runs
each, mean  stddev, 2% producible:

                            rc5            posted        requested
    ops/s                   4751  684     5181  18     5206  84
    PSI some, mean %        28.7  11.5    22.0  0      22.0  0
    PSI some, peak avg10    42.8  30.7    24.9  0.3    25.0  0.8
    s with some avg10 > 50  3.3  5.8      0             0
    give-ups (NOFRAG off)   0              222  58      277  199
    movable blocks lost     641  13       654  10      652  14
    whole blocks claimed    90  8         81  10       76  8

rc5 stormed in one of its three runs: 3.85M order-9 reclaim runs in
180s, PSI at 42% with ten seconds above 50, workers that would not die
on SIGKILL. The other two were quiet, which matches a workload that
OOMs regularly rather than always. The fixed kernels never stormed.

Between the two floors there is no difference I can measure here: same
PSI, same throughput, same give-ups, same movable blocks lost, same
whole blocks produced.

The promoted path is a small part of what the allocator does in this
workload, 16-22k order-9 reclaim runs against a million order-0 ones for
page cache, and a few hundred give-ups in 180s.

---

Same movable blocks lost and same whole blocks produced in all three
kernels, so in this workload the extra SYNC_FULL passes neither produce
blocks nor save any.

---

That shows up only when I take the I/O out: tmpfs, every block pinned,
1M empty files. Then every exhausted order-0 refill does a whole-zone
SYNC_FULL pass before it falls back, PSI some runs at 39% against 20%,
and the churn takes 1.3-2.8x as long, five runs each.

What do you prefer here? I don't have strong preference either way.

[1] One thing the pins made me notice. A FOLL_LONGTERM pin migrates
    the page first only for ZONE_MOVABLE, CMA and isolated blocks, see
    folio_is_longterm_pinnable(); a page in a MIGRATE_MOVABLE block in
    ZONE_NORMAL is pinned where it sits, and the block can never be
    made whole for as long as the pin lives. The migration target in
    gup already uses GFP_USER without __GFP_MOVABLE, so a moved page
    lands in a non-movable block.

    Should defrag_mode treat MIGRATE_MOVABLE like ZONE_MOVABLE there and
    move the page out at pin time? Ideally we might want to move it back
    on unpin, but it can be done by compaction too.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 01/13] mm/khugepaged: drop redundant mm_struct pin in madvise_collapse()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes an unnecessary mmgrab() reference in the madvise_collapse() function, which is already holding a valid mm_users reference. The redundant mmgrab() call is dropped to simplify the code and avoid potential issues.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 02/13] mm/khugepaged: count collapses where khugepaged makes them
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged functionality to count collapses where it makes them, rather than relying on the caller to increment a shared counter. The daemon can now keep its own counter without needing to test who called the collapse function. This change simplifies the code and improves maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 03/13] mm/khugepaged: rename mthp_present_ptes bitmap to eligible_ptes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the bitmap 'mthp_present_ptes' in the mm/khugepaged module to 'eligible_ptes'. The name change reflects that a set bit in this bitmap indicates not only that a PTE is present, but also that it has passed various checks. This change does not introduce any functional changes and is intended to improve clarity of the code.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 04/13] mm/collapse: add collapse.h for the collapse interface
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new header file, mm/collapse.h, to separate the interface and implementation of the collapse feature from the khugepaged.c file. The collapse feature is used for page migration and memory compaction. The new header file defines an enum for scan results and a struct for control parameters, as well as two constants related to page table entries. This separation improves code organization and maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 05/13] mm/collapse: state what a collapse may do in the policy
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new struct called collapse_policy to store the policy decisions made by the caller before asking for a collapse. The policy includes limits on missing, swapped-out or shared PTEs in a window, as well as other settings such as whether to look at used ranges and how to handle MADV_FREE'd pages. The patch replaces scattered tests throughout the collapse path with reads from the collapse_policy struct, simplifying the code and removing the need for khugepaged to look up who called it. The policy is filled once per scan pass by khugepaged and once per call by MADV_COLLAPSE.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the call to collapse_file() from collapse_scan_file() to collapse_single_pmd(). review_comments.summary:
Author acknowledges David's feedback about virtual address scanning not being the best way to collapse page cache, but considers it out of scope for this patchset

Author explained that collapse_single_pmd() dropping the lock requires knowing which lock the caller took, and proposed adding a flag to indicate this, similar to the existing lock_dropped bool.

The author agrees that khugepaged has worked since a specific commit to walk tables under one hold, giving the lock up only to collapse, and confirms this behavior will be kept in the patch series.

Author responded to David's feedback by explaining that their version of the patch has a lower overhead than the original, citing measurements on a production config and arguing that the additional cost is acceptable given the bounded nature of the scan.

Author responded to David's feedback by explaining that khugepaged's scan rate is a critical concern for their use case, and they cannot afford to sacrifice it for the sake of having a single entry point into the engine.

Author acknowledges the appeal of a single entry point but disagrees that it's worth the cost, specifically citing negative impacts on locking and scan rate.
review_comments.raw_body:
Right on both.

As I mentioned before, virtual address scanning might not be the best
way to collapse page cache.

We might want to start from inodes on superblocks that have large folios
enabled.

But it is out of scope for the patchset.

---

That is the reason the caller owns the lock here.

On top of this series I have khugepaged scanning under the per-VMA lock:
the scan asserts whatever lock the caller holds, the caller does
vma_end_read() before the run, and the run takes the locks it needs
itself.

Neither the scan nor the run changed for it.

With collapse_single_pmd() dropping the lock, it has to know which lock
the caller took. process_madvise() on another process's mm cannot move
to the VMA lock: untagged_addr_remote() asserts mmap_lock, so a remote
MADV_COLLAPSE keeps it while a local one and khugepaged move on.

The single call would need a flag saying which lock to drop. That is
the lock_dropped bool again, pointing the other way.

---

Yes, we should.

Walking the tables under one hold and giving the lock up only to
collapse is how khugepaged has worked since ba76149f47d8 ("thp:
khugepaged").

The bool is just how that signal got plumbed when MADV_COLLAPSE arrived
in 50ad2f24b3b4, and it has already cost one bug, 5a62019807da
("mm/khugepaged: fix issue with tracking lock").

This series removes the bool and keeps the behaviour.

---

The rwsem and the VMA lookup are not the only cost.

In your version every table is a visit to the mm: unlock,
khugepaged_mm_lock, back through khugepaged_do_scan(),
khugepaged_mm_lock again, a trylock and a VMA walk, for a scan that on
memory already huge is one pmd read.

I measured your prototype against patch 9 as posted, both on a production
config, 8G of anonymous memory already collapsed, scan_sleep_millisecs 0,
pages_to_scan 65536, PMD order only, five runs each, medians:

                                     as posted    yours
  khugepaged, nothing to collapse:
    full passes over 8G in 20s         251,180    55,477
    khugepaged CPU                        100%      100%
    cost per refused table               19 ns     88 ns
  MADV_COLLAPSE, already huge:
    512M per call, p50                  3.8 us   17.4 us
    2M per call, p50                    703 ns    703 ns
  tables walked in full then refused
    (max_ptes_none 0), passes in 20s       803       836

On being nice to the rest of the system: the scan is already bounded.
The read hold ends after pages_to_scan worth of progress. We already
have properly sized scan batching in place.

---

khugepaged matters. We run it across the fleet, and its scan cost is
what decides how aggressive we can afford to be with it. I am not
giving up scan rate to keep one entry point into the engine.

For a single PMD there is no difference either way. For a range, today a
MADV_COLLAPSE over memory that is already huge walks it without letting
go of the lock at all; in your version it relocks and revalidates for
every table, and tells madvise_walk_vmas() to look the VMA up again.

---

I see the appeal of the single entry point for the collapse engine. I do.

But it costs us on both the locking picture and the scan rate. That
does not work for me.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 11/13] mm/collapse: work out the orders a VMA allows once per VMA
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the way the kernel handles memory collapsing by allowing it to work out the allowed orders for a VMA only once per VMA, rather than once per PTE table. This is done by passing the mask of allowed orders from collapse_possible_orders() directly to the functions that need it, and sampling it once per VMA instead of once per table. The patch also ensures that changes to hugepage_vma_revalidate() are properly handled under the lock that produced the mask.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 12/13] mm/collapse: declare the collapse interface in collapse.h
series_items.patch_summary: This patch declares the collapse interface in collapse.h, which includes functions and variables related to collapsing huge pages. The interface is designed to be used by a caller that holds the mmap_lock for reading, and it involves three main steps: setting up control, scanning PTE tables, and running the collapse. The patch also renames hugepage_vma_revalidate() to collapse_vma_revalidate() and adds documentation comments to explain the purpose and behavior of each function. This is a preparation step for implementing MADV_COLLAPSE in madvise.c.

review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

[ This is the first of the cleanups I said I would front-load ]

There is no line between the collapse engine and the callers that ask for
a collapse.  khugepaged.c holds both, and they reach into each other.

 - Sixteen tests through the collapse path read cc->is_khugepaged to work
   out what they are allowed to do, when every one of those decisions was
   made by the caller before it asked.

 - collapse_single_pmd() does both halves of a collapse behind one call and
   drops mmap_lock somewhere in the middle.  Which of its paths dropped it
   is not something a caller can see, so it hands back a bool and the
   caller keeps track.

 - MADV_COLLAPSE's implementation -- the walk over the user's range, the
   per-PMD loop, the errno translation -- sits in khugepaged.c, which is
   the daemon's file.

So: draw the line.  State what a caller allows in a policy, split the call
in two with the lock as the boundary, and move the syscall to madvise.c.
What the engine offers is then three calls, with the lock state written
down against each, and a policy the caller fills for itself:

    collapse_control_init(cc)         once, before the first table
    collapse_policy_*(&cc->policy)    what this caller allows
    collapse_scan_pmd(vma, addr, ...) per table, under mmap_lock
    collapse_run_pmd(mm, addr, ...)   when a scan found work, no mmap_lock

The engine stays in khugepaged.c for now; what changes is that it has an
interface, and that neither half has to ask about the other.  madvise.c
gains the operation it should have had all along.

Changes since v3
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260916093145.4022188-1-kirill@shutemov.name/

 - Patch 5: the PTE limits come as two sets, struct collapse_limits for a
   PMD-sized window and one for anything smaller, and the strict_sub_pmd
   flag goes.  The warning for a max_ptes_none between 0 and the maximum
   moves to where khugepaged fills its policy.  The fields only one side
   reads are prefixed anon_ or file_.  collapse_policy_forced() is
   collapse_policy_madvise() (David).

 - Patch 8 is new: collapse_file() is called from collapse_single_pmd()
   rather than from inside collapse_scan_file(), so the file scan stops at
   the decision before the scan/run split.  The writeback retry and the
   tracepoint change move into it, so patch 9 is only the split (David).

 - Patch 9: no collapse_control_release().  It had nothing to release in
   this series; it comes back with the engine, where init allocates.  The
   check that the last scan was run stays at the top of collapse_scan_pmd()
   (David).

 - Patch 10: the changelog says why the lock boundary belongs to the
   caller (David).

 - Patch 11: both callers pass their TVA type as the literal it is rather
   than reading it back from the policy (David).

 - Patch 12: kerneldoc on every function collapse.h declares (David).

 - Acked-by from David Hildenbrand on 1-4, 6 and 7; Reviewed-by from
   Baolin Wang on 10.  Reviewed-by dropped from 5 and 9, which changed.

Changes since v2
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260910120238.2529819-1-kirill@shutemov.name/

 - Patch 8: the file scan returns SCAN_PTE_MAPPED_HUGEPAGE as it is and
   the run is handed what the scan returned, so it goes straight to
   retracting the PTE table when it sees it.  The scan_retract_only flag
   and the result round trip go, and the two copies of the file put become
   one helper (Zi).  Patches 9-12 follow the new signature.

 - Patch 8: mthp_collapse() and collapse_huge_page() read the orders and
   the referenced and swapped-out counts from collapse_control instead of
   taking them as arguments (Baolin).

 - Patch 11: each interface function is documented where it is defined,
   with the lock state on entry and exit.  The overview in collapse.h
   stays (Zi).

 - Reviewed-by from Zi Yan on 8 and 9, and from Zi Yan and Baolin Wang
   on 5 and 10.

Changes since v1
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/cover.1788533997.git.kas@kernel.org/

 - Rebased onto mm-new with Vernon Yang's tracepoint fixes in it.  Patch 8
   no longer merges the two calls to each scan tracepoint, since the base
   already has one; its changelog now says what the status field reports.

 - Patch 3: nr_occupied_ptes is nr_eligible_ptes, and the mthp_collapse()
   comment counts eligible PTEs too (Zi, Baolin).

 - Patch 4: no comments on the two constants (Baolin).

 - Patch 5: one line per policy field (Baolin).

 - Patch 8: the file side is split like the anonymous one (Zi).
   collapse_scan_file() runs under mmap_lock in the scan and only reads;
   collapse_file() runs in the run.  See Behaviour below.

 - Reviewed-by from Zi Yan and Baolin Wang on 1-4, 6 and 7.

Patches
=======

The first three stand alone and can be taken separately:

  1  drop the mmgrab() MADV_COLLAPSE has held since 7d8faaf15545
  2  count collapses in khugepaged's own walk, where the daemon's
     bookkeeping belongs
  3  rename cc->mthp_present_ptes to eligible_ptes, which is what a set
     bit means

Then the interface, in order:

  4  add collapse.h, and move enum scan_result, struct collapse_control
     and the two constants into it
  5  struct collapse_policy, filled by the caller; the is_khugepaged
     tests become field reads, and the flag goes
  6  drop collapse_possible(), a wrapper that only turns a mask into a bool
  7  collapse_control_init_scan() is a per-table reset, so name it
     collapse_scan_reset()
  8  call collapse_file() from collapse_single_pmd(), so the file scan
     stops at the decision
  9  give the scan and the collapse a function each: collapse_scan_pmd()
     and collapse_run_pmd()
 10  open-code the entry point that joined them, so each caller owns the
     lock across the boundary and the bool goes
 11  work out the orders a VMA allows once per VMA, not once per table
 12  declare the three calls in collapse.h, with the lock rules
 13  MADV_COLLAPSE moves to madvise.c

Behaviour
=========

No functional change is intended.  Nothing here changes which tables get
collapsed, into what, or what MADV_COLLAPSE returns.  The tracepoints are
the one place a change can be seen from outside; the rest is where work
happens, not what it does.

 - Patches 8 and 9: mm_khugepaged_scan_file and mm_khugepaged_scan_pmd
   fire before the collapse rather than after it.  For an accepted table
   their status field reads SCAN_SUCCEED, where it used to carry what the
   collapse made of the table; that is now for mm_khugepaged_collapse_file
   and mm_collapse_huge_page to report.

Four things move that a reader should not have to find in the diff:

 - Patch 5: khugepaged fills its policy once per scan pass, so the
   max_ptes_* limits and the defrag setting behind the allocation mask are
   sampled once per pass rather than once per table.  A knob written
   mid-pass takes effect on the next pass instead of the next table.

 - Patch 8: the writeback retry re-runs collapse_file() alone, where it
   used to rescan the page cache first.

 - Patch 9: the file scan runs under mmap_lock, where before the lock was
   given up first.  A file table the scan refuses no longer costs
   khugepaged an unlock, a trip back through khugepaged_do_scan(), a
   relock and a VMA lookup; only a table it goes on to collapse does.

 - Patch 11: which orders a table is scanned for is sampled once per VMA
   rather than once per table.  It cannot widen what a collapse does; the
   order is tested again under the lock the collapse retakes.

For an anonymous table, and for a file table that gets collapsed, the lock
is given up and taken again at exactly the points it was before; the only
difference is that the caller is the one doing it.

DEBUG_VM config, in the five forms run_vmtests.sh runs it.  Every patch
builds, CONFIG_TRANSPARENT_HUGEPAGE=n included.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the tight coupling between the users of collapse and its machinery in khugepaged.c, agreeing to separate them by introducing a new header file mm/collapse.h that defines common types and constants used by both sides. This change is non-functional.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern about the complexity of collapse_single_pmd() by splitting it into two functions: collapse_scan_pmd() and collapse_run_pmd(). The new functions are designed to work together, with collapse_scan_pmd() scanning for potential collapses and collapse_run_pmd() performing the actual collapse. The author also moved the anonymous scan under mmap_lock with the file scan, reducing the number of times the lock is taken.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed David Hildenbrand's concern about the PTE limits being set differently for PMD and sub-PMD windows by introducing a new struct collapse_policy that allows callers to specify their own policy, including PTE limits. The khugepaged code will fill in this policy once per scan pass, while MADV_COLLAPSE will do so once per call. This change does not alter the behavior of khugepaged but rather simplifies the logic by removing the need for the collapse code to look up who called it.

review_comments.author: David (Arm)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer David (Arm) noted that the patch changes the behavior of khugepaged by sampling max_ptes_* limits and defrag setting once per pass instead of on every table, which is a change in behavior. He also acknowledged two other changes as not actually required for the original call to collapse_file() from collapse_single_pmd().

review_comments.author: Andrew Morton
review_comments.summary: Andrew Morton requested that the collapse engine be separated from its callers, specifically suggesting that khugepaged.c hold only one half of a collapse and that the other half be moved to madvise.c. He proposed drawing a clear line between the two by introducing an interface for the engine and splitting the call into three parts: initialization, policy setting, and scanning/running.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Zi Yan noted that the original patch did not properly separate the scanning and running of collapses, with collapse_single_pmd() doing both jobs in the middle of a function. He suggested splitting this into two functions: collapse_scan_pmd(), which scans one table, and collapse_run_pmd(), which does the actual collapse work.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 1/2] iommu/arm-smmu-v3: Add a cmdq_max_n_shift module parameter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new module parameter, cmdq_max_n_shift, which allows users to cap the command queue depth as a logarithmic value of the number of entries. The default value is set to the hardware maximum, but can be overridden by setting this parameter. This change aims to provide more flexibility and control over memory allocation for systems with multiple SMMUv3 instances or tight memory budgets.

review_comments.summary: Applied the patch and added Tested-by and Reviewed-by tags. The change looks good to me.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, Sep 25, 2026 at 03:15:29PM +0100, Kiryl Shutsemau wrote:
> From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>
> 
> The command queue depth comes straight from the maximum the hardware
> advertises in IDR1, which reaches megabytes of coherent DMA per queue.
> A system with several SMMUv3 instances pays that per instance, and the
> Tegra241 CMDQV pays it again for every VCMDQ it preallocates.
> 
> Queue depth only bounds how many commands may be in flight before a sync.
> A machine driving a handful of devices, or one with a tight memory budget,
> has no use for the maximum, and no way to say so.
> 
> Add cmdq_max_n_shift, a cap on the depth given as the log2 of the entry
> count, the form the hardware itself takes in the LOG2SIZE field of
> CMDQ_BASE. It defaults to the largest depth the driver allocates, so an
> unset parameter changes nothing. Decide the depth in
> arm_smmu_cmdq_max_n_shift(), which applies the parameter to the IDR1
> value, so the queue is allocated at the requested size. The Tegra241 CMDQV
> sizes its VCMDQs from IDR1 itself, so route that through the same helper.
> 
> Floor the request at one page worth of entries. Without the floor, a small
> request trips the CMDQ_BATCH_ENTRIES check in arm_smmu_device_hw_probe()
> and the SMMU fails to probe. The floor also costs nothing: coherent DMA is
> page granular, so a shallower queue occupies the same memory as one that
> fills the page.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series makes the queue depths in the ARM SMMUv3 IOMMU tunable, allowing them to be adjusted based on system requirements. The queues are currently sized from the IDR1 maximum and allocated at probe, which can consume megabytes of memory per queue per SMMU instance. In a kdump kernel, this can lead to out-of-memory errors due to limited crashkernel reservations. The patch series introduces a module parameter cmdq_max_n_shift that allows the command queue depth to be adjusted, and applies it in non-kdump kernels. This reduces the memory consumption of the queues from megabytes to kilobytes, allowing kdump kernels to save vmcores successfully.

A specific problem addressed by this patch is the kernfs notify worker, which can be stuck while holding the cgroup2 kernfs_rwsem lock. The patch adds a new policy called high_policy that allows policies to specify where memory.high should be enforced instead of inlining the call. Measurements show significant improvements in performance and latency compared to the baseline and an existing fix for a similar problem.

>
> This is the first series of memcg_ext, proposed at [1].  It adds
> bpf_memcg_ops, a struct_ops type through which memory controller policy is
> attached to a cgroup.  A charge runs the policies of its cgroup and of
> every ancestor, and the kernel combines what they return.  BPF picks
> between things the kernel already does; it never does the work itself and
> never touches a page counter.
>
> The plan is to grow this one member at a time, and to add a member only
> when there is a concrete problem it solves and a measurement showing it
> does.  Nothing is added because it might be useful later.  So this first
> series adds one member, for one problem.
>
> The problem
> ===========
>
> try_charge_memcg() calls __mem_cgroup_handle_over_high() before it returns,
> which reclaims and can throttle the task.  That happens wherever the charge
> happens, so a task holding a kernel lock can be stuck there, and everything
> waiting on that lock is stuck behind it.
>
> One concrete scenario which can be resolved by this new feature is the
> kernfs notify worker. It delivers notifications with the cgroup2
> kernfs_rwsem held for read, and the charge for the delivery allocation goes
> to the cgroup that set the watch, usually one already under pressure. So
> the worker reclaims while holding the lock, a waiting writer blocks every
> later reader, and anything touching cgroupfs stalls for seconds. The patch
> proposed in [2] fixes that one path in the kernel only for kernfs_rwsem.
> The same path still takes kernfs_supers_rwsem.
>
> One can make an argument that if we know the source of the issue in the
> kernel, why not fix it similarly to [2] instead of having a generic
> solution? The reason is that it will be an uphill and continuous battle as
> the kernel keeps evolving and new sources of lock holders doing allocations
> keep coming up. In addition, there will be cases where it might not be
> possible to move the allocations out of locks, or where doing so would
> make the code really ugly [3].
>
> high_policy() lets a policy say where memory.high should be enforced
> instead.  Its one request, BPF_MEMCG_HIGH_DEFER_INLINE, skips the inline
> call, leaving the debt to be paid at the return to userspace.
>
> Results
> =======
>
> Measured on a kernel without [2], with a policy that marks cgroupfs kernfs
> lock holders.  Reproducer at [4].
>
>                                       baseline    policy    upstream fix
>   max kernfs_rwsem hold, worker        2.049 s     199 us   not taken
>   max kernfs_supers_rwsem hold         2.049 s     4.8 ms   2.056 s
>   max kernfs_rwsem write wait          4.096 s     6.2 ms   8.7 ms
>   walker passes over /sys/fs/cgroup        352       5711   6700
>   churn mkdir+rmdir ops                 13 059    364 832   415 488
>   churn max latency                     30.7 s    15.1 ms   12.7 ms
>
> The policy matches the fix on the bystander numbers, and does better on
> kernfs_supers_rwsem, which the fix does not help: it drops kernfs_rwsem
> from the delivery loop, while the policy stops the worker stalling at all,
> so every lock it holds benefits.
>

> ===========
>
> Patch 1 is a build fix.  __cgroup_bpf_query() only works because
> CGROUP_TCP_SOCK_OPS is the one struct_ops attach type; a second one breaks
> the build and makes a query for type 0 return the wrong thing.
>
> Patch 2 adds the type and its registration, with no members, so nothing is
> dispatched and behaviour does not change.  It also moves the attach type
> enum out of CONFIG_CGROUP_BPF and fixes the register_bpf_struct_ops() no-op
> stub, which never compiled because no caller reached it.
>
> Patch 3 adds high_policy() and wires it into try_charge_memcg().
>
> Patch 4 is the sample.  It tracks the two cgroupfs kernfs locks by hooking
> the rwsem primitives rather than the forty-odd functions that take them.
>
> Known open questions
> ====================
>
> The semantics of memory.high for remote chargers or kernel threads is a
> grey area and this series does not aim to resolve that.
>
> Another open question is whether a bound on debt deferral is needed. At
> the moment, we think that rather than putting a limit on deferral for
> memory.high, it will be better to handle that through an async worker like
> memcg->high_work.  We aim to introduce that later, along with the right CPU
> accounting for that async work.

On the open question of how deferred debt eventually gets paid: would
it make sense for the policy to also notify userspace (e.g. via
ringbuf) when it defers, and have a userspace reclaimer do the reclaim
through memory.reclaim?

accounting. If the concern is that the kworker's CPU usage is not
charged to the target cgroup, the userspace reclaimer could instead be
spawned with clone3(CLONE_INTO_CGROUP) so it runs inside the target
cgroup, and both its CPU and memory usage get charged there.

constraint cannot take processes, so this would only work for leaf
cgroups.

> ("memcg: synchronously enforce memory.high for large overcharges") because
> it has introduced more problems than it has solved, but that is a separate
> topic. The initial commit already mentioned that MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH was used
> arbitrarily, so replacing it with something big might be acceptable. I want
> to keep that decision separate.

Which kernel paths allocate enough for this to matter? Can you give specific
examples where the in-kernel synchronous enforcement helps?

> Returning to the actual proposal, my plan was to start small with a narrow,
> specific use case. However, my long-term plan is to provide a mechanism to
> change the default behavior for custom use cases. For example, for
> memory.high, I will provide a way for users to specify what behavior they
> want, i.e., whether or not they want more synchronous throttling.

This doesn't seem like a policy problem. It feels like a problem that should
be and can reasonably be solved for everybody, so I'm not sure whether BPF is
the right call for this specific purpose.

Thanks.

--
tejun

---

Hello, Shakeel.

On Wed, Sep 30, 2026 at 06:00:41PM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> mlock(), madvise(POPULATE), fadvise(WILLNEED) are the obvious ones where large
> amount of memory can be allocated before returning to userspace.

These are explicit bulk memory operations running in the calling task's own
context, so they can be special-cased. Each is a loop with points between
chunks where no locks are held, and the same over-high handler the
return-to-userspace path runs can run there. That keeps the throttling on
the task which asked for the memory and can't cause priority inversions. The
set of such paths is small and obvious, so I don't think it'd be onerous to
maintain.

> > This doesn't seem like a policy problem.
>
> What is "This" in the above statement?

The whole thing, how memory.high should be enforced when the overrun happens
inside the kernel or from a kthread.

> Here if you meant that default behavior of memory.high should work for most (if
> not all) users then we are on same page. If some user want memory.high reclaim
> to happen in a separate thread instead of return-to-userspace or synchronously,
> this proposal provides mechanism through BPF to such users to achieve their
> goals.

I think there's a common reasonable solution here, which is deciding by who
the charge is for. A task charging for itself gets return-to-userspace
enforcement plus the checks in the explicit bulk operations above. A kthread
or anything else charging on behalf of a cgroup shouldn't be throttled for
the cgroup's overrun. The overrun is attributed to the cgroup, async reclaim
is kicked, and the cgroup's own tasks absorb the throttling on their next
return to userspace. The in-charge synchronous fallback goes away. Each case
has one reasonable answer, so I don't see a policy choice to expose here.

Thanks.

--
tejun

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 04/30] powerpc: mm: add PMD swap-exclusive helpers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds PMD (Page Middle Directory) swap-exclusive helpers for the PowerPC architecture. The goal is to enable keeping a PMD-mapped anonymous THP (Transparent Huge Page) mapped across a swap round-trip, which requires the PG_anon_exclusive flag to survive in a swap PMD. The patch introduces three new macros: pmd_swp_mkexclusive, pmd_swp_exclusive, and pmd_swp_clear_exclusive, which wrap the existing PTE (Page Table Entry) helpers.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 05/30] riscv: mm: add PMD swap-exclusive helpers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds PMD swap-exclusive helpers for the RISC-V architecture, allowing a PMD-mapped anonymous THP to be kept mapped across a swap round-trip. The new helpers wrap existing PTE ones and reuse the _PAGE_SWP_EXCLUSIVE flag, enabling efficient handling of swap operations in PMDs.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 06/30] s390: mm: add PMD swap-exclusive helpers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds PMD swap-exclusive helpers for the s390 architecture, allowing a PMD-mapped anonymous THP to be kept mapped across a swap round-trip by introducing an exclusive bit in the RSTE swap layout. This is necessary because on s390, a swap PMD is not just a swap PTE in disguise, but has its own unique layout. The patch introduces new macros and functions to set and clear this exclusive bit, enabling more efficient handling of swap operations on s390 systems.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 07/30] x86: mm: add PMD swap-exclusive helpers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds helpers for managing PMD-mapped anonymous huge pages (THPs) that are swapped out and then brought back in. The new helpers, which reuse the existing _PAGE_SWP_EXCLUSIVE bit, allow a PMD-mapped THP to be kept mapped across a swap round-trip. This is necessary because x86-64 encodes swap PMDs exactly like swap PTEs, and 32-bit x86 has different behavior for this bit. The patch adds assertions to ensure that the helpers are only used on architectures that support them.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 08/30] mm: recognize PMD swap entries in the softleaf layer
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the softleaf layer in the Linux kernel to recognize and handle PMD swap entries. It introduces a new function `pmd_is_swap_entry()` that checks if a PMD entry encodes a swap entry, and updates existing functions to correctly handle swap entries. The changes include removing unnecessary checks for migration and device-private entries, and adding a check for swap entries in the `softleaf_is_valid_pmd_entry()` function. This patch prepares the kernel for installing swap entries directly into the PMD layer.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 09/30] mm/debug_vm_pgtable: test PMD swap-exclusive helpers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a test for PMD (Page Map Directory) swap-exclusive helpers to the Linux kernel's debug_vm_pgtable module. The test is designed to catch architectures that have chosen a PMD exclusive bit overlapping with the swap type or offset field, which would otherwise only be detected by data corruption at runtime. The test mirrors existing pte_swap_exclusive_tests() and checks for correct behavior of PMD swap-exclusive helpers in various scenarios. This patch addresses a potential issue where certain architectures may not correctly handle swap-exclusive bits in PMDs.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 10/30] mm: make PMD migration-entry splitting explicit
series_items.patch_summary: This patch makes the splitting of PMD migration entries explicit by renaming the 'freeze' boolean in __split_huge_pmd() to 'to_migration_entries'. It also introduces a new function split_pmd_to_migration_entries() for use by try_to_migrate_one(). The patch asserts that only present or device-private PMDs are handed to this function. No functional changes are intended, and the patch is part of a larger series of 30 patches.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 11/30] mm: split PMD swap entries into PTE swap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits PMD swap entries into PTE swap entries in the Linux kernel's memory management system. The goal is to allow operations that split a PMD, such as mprotect() or munmap(), to also handle swap entries. This is achieved by adding a new branch in the __split_huge_pmd_locked() function to handle swap PMDs and convert them into PTEs. The patch also removes unnecessary reference counting for swap entries and adds tests to ensure that the correct snapshot of the old PMD is used during the conversion process.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 12/30] mm/swap: allow duplicating a range of swap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows duplicating a range of swap entries at once, rather than one slot at a time. This is necessary because the PMD swap entry fork path requires multiple slots to be duplicated simultaneously, and doing it one slot at a time would require acquiring and releasing the cluster lock multiple times. The patch introduces new functions `swap_dup_entries_direct` and `swap_retry_table_alloc_nr` that take an additional argument for the number of entries to duplicate, and renames existing functions to inline wrappers. The range of swap entries must be within one cluster, and attempting to duplicate a crossing range will result in an error.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 13/30] mm: handle PMD swap entries in fork path
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where PMD swap entries are not handled correctly in the fork path, leading to duplicated and unreferenced page table slots. The patch introduces a new function `copy_huge_non_present_pmd` that duplicates PMD swap entries by creating new references to the underlying pages and updating the mm counter accordingly. It also updates the `copy_huge_pmd` function to handle GFP_ATOMIC allocation failures for extend-tables, allowing the fork process to retry with GFP_KERNEL. The patch further refactors the code to move the mm counter update into each entry-type arm, improving consistency and accuracy in page table management.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 14/30] mm: zswap: reject high-order swap cache allocations backed by zswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch rejects high-order swap cache allocations backed by zswap when the range of swap slots is split between zswap entries and the backing device. This prevents a disk read from returning stale or zero data for every slot zswap owns. The check is done after the folio is in the swap cache, ensuring that the answer is stable. If a high-order allocation over such a range is attempted, it will be rejected with an -EBUSY error.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 15/30] mm: swap in PMD swap entries as whole THPs during swapoff
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the behavior of the swapoff operation to handle PMD (Page Map Directory) swap entries as whole THPs (Transparent Huge Pages). The existing implementation would only consider PTEs, leading to incomplete swapoff operations. The patch introduces a new function `swap_pmd_cache_lookup` to classify PMD swap entries and map them back in as one THP, preserving soft-dirty, exclusive, and UFFD state. If the PMD entry is split or has per-page zswap state, it falls back to PTE handling.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 16/30] fs/proc: account PMD swap entries in smaps
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the smaps functionality in the Linux kernel to correctly account for PMD swap entries. It introduces a new function, smaps_account_swap(), which is called when a swapped-out THP is encountered. This function calculates the correct Swap and SwapPss values based on the swap reference counts of each slot in the PMD entry. The patch also updates the smaps_pte_entry() and smaps_pmd_entry() functions to use this new function, ensuring that device-private PMD entries are treated as fake-present and allowing for accurate PSS and private/shared accounting.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 17/30] mm: handle soft-dirty and uffd-wp on PMD swap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the Linux kernel to correctly handle soft-dirty and uffd-wp flags on PMD swap entries, ensuring that these flags are properly updated during page table operations. The changes affect several functions in fs/proc/task_mmu.c and mm/huge_memory.c, where the code now checks for both migration and swap entries when updating these flags. This patch addresses a problem where clearing soft-dirty would skip swapped-out THPs, UFFDIO_WRITEPROTECT would not arm it, and mremap would not mark the destination correctly.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 18/30] mm/hmm: fault PMD swap entries on demand
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the handling of absent PMD entries in the Linux kernel's Heterogeneous Memory Management (HMM) module. When a swapped-out huge page is encountered, it will no longer be reported as an error, but instead treated like a PTE swap entry and recorded as such when a fault occurs. This change ensures that memory that needs to be paged in is properly identified and handled.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 19/30] mm: free PMD swap entries in zap_huge_pmd()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the zap_huge_pmd() function to handle PMD swap entries before attempting to access a folio. It checks if the cleared PMD is a swap entry and, if so, frees the associated swap slots and updates the memory management counters accordingly.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 20/30] mm/madvise: free PMD swap entries with MADV_FREE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's memory management to free PMD swap entries when using the MADV_FREE advisory. Currently, madvise_free_pte_range() only frees present THP pages and ignores swapped-out pages. The patch introduces a new approach where it checks if the entire PMD is covered by the advice and, if so, frees all its slots at once. Otherwise, it splits the range into smaller sub-ranges that can be handled by the PTE path. This change ensures that MADV_FREE over a swapped-out THP silently does nothing, which was the previous behavior.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 21/30] mm/madvise: skip PMD swap entries for MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of PMD swap entries for MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT operations in the Linux kernel's mm/madvise module. It skips unnecessary processing when a swapped-out huge page (THP) has no resident folio to deactivate or reclaim, preventing potential issues with migration or device-private entries. The patch introduces a check for PMD swap entries before attempting to map PTE tables, ensuring efficient and correct handling of these operations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 22/30] mm/madvise: keep PMD swap entries whole for MADV_GUARD_INSTALL/REMOVE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the MADV_GUARD_INSTALL and REMOVE callbacks in the Linux kernel to handle PMD swap entries correctly. Currently, these callbacks test for huge pages using pmd_trans_huge(), but this is false for PMD swap entries, leading to incorrect behavior when trying to install or remove guard pages. The patch adds a check for PMD swap entries using pmd_is_swap_entry() and returns immediately if the entry is swapped out, preventing unnecessary splitting of the page table.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 23/30] mm/mincore: report PMD swap-cache residency
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the mincore function where it incorrectly reports huge PMD pages as resident when they are actually swapped out. The patch introduces a new function, mincore_pmd_swap, which looks up the swap cache for PMD-sized folios and returns residency information for each page within that range. If the PMD-sized folio was split while its entry remained in the swap cache, the function falls back to looking up each covered slot individually. The patch also adds a new check to handle PMD swap entries without CONFIG_THP_SWAP enabled.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 24/30] mm/khugepaged: treat PMD swap entries as mapped THPs
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged code to treat PMD swap entries as mapped THPs, allowing them to be handled similarly to present huge PMDs. This change affects how MADV_COLLAPSE handles swapped-out THPs, ensuring that they are still collapsed into a single THP on first touch. The approach taken is to add a new condition in the check_pmd_state function to return SCAN_PMD_MAPPED for PMD swap entries.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 25/30] mm: handle PMD swap entries in MADV_WILLNEED
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves handling of PMD swap entries in MADV_WILLNEED operations by prefetching the whole range as one PMD-order folio instead of walking PTEs individually. This approach avoids issues with order-0 readahead and subsequent faults, and ensures that the eventual fault still takes do_huge_pmd_swap_page(). The patch also checks the THP policy before reading at PMD order to prevent handing do_swap_page() a PMD-sized folio to map with PTEs. If the prefetch fails or if the PMD is split, the patch falls back to the PTE path, which can still read the slots at order 0.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 26/30] mm: handle PMD swap entries in UFFDIO_MOVE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for moving PMD-level swap entries in UFFDIO_MOVE operations. It introduces a new function, move_swap_pmd(), which moves the entry under both PMD locks and propagates soft-dirty flags. The function also handles revalidation of cached folios and anchors the anon rmap to the destination VMA. Additionally, it rejects PMD swap entries at the destination with -EEXIST. This patch addresses a problem where aligned UFFDIO_MOVE operations over swapped-out THPs fail due to missing support for PMD-level swap entries.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 27/30] mm: don't PTE-batch a swap-in over a hardware-poisoned subpage
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents the PTE-batching mechanism from mapping a swap-in over a hardware-poisoned subpage, which could lead to undetected faults. The problem arises because the batching path doesn't check for poisoned subpages individually, allowing a faulting page to be mapped even if one of its subpages is poisoned. To fix this, the patch adds a check to ensure that each subpage is tested separately before mapping the folio, using the `folio_has_hwpoisoned_subpage` function to detect poisoned subpages.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 28/30] mm: handle PMD swap entry faults on swap-in
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a problem where PMD (Page Map Directory) swap entries would fault indefinitely when trying to swap in a huge page. The patch introduces a new function, do_huge_pmd_swap_page(), which resolves the whole mapping at PMD granularity and handles various failure cases, such as cache splitting or allocation failures. It also ensures that the folio is properly dropped from the swap cache if it has never been mapped or is not up-to-date. The patch aims to prevent a transient PMD-order allocation failure from becoming a VM_FAULT_OOM error.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 29/30] mm: install PMD swap entries on swap-out
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the handling of PMD-mapped anonymous huge pages (THPs) during swap-out operations. When a THP is swapped out, it was previously split into smaller mappings, which caused performance issues and unnecessary overhead. This patch introduces a new approach where a single PMD-level swap entry is installed for each contiguous run of slots in the swap cache, eliminating the need for splitting and reducing the number of faults during swap-in. The patch also updates various kernel components to support this new behavior, including the huge memory management code, rmap, vmscan, and vmstat.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 30/30] selftests/mm: add PMD swap entry tests
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds tests for PMD (Page Map Directory) swap entry functionality in the Linux kernel. The tests cover various scenarios, including swapping out a THP (Transparent Huge Page) and verifying that the thp_swpout_pmd counter is increased accordingly. The patch also includes code to read /proc/vmstat fields and register the pmd_swap test with the default runner. It supports both synchronous and asynchronous swap devices and handles cases where zswap is enabled. The tests are designed to be skipped if the kernel does not implement PMD swap entries or if it lacks a thp_swpout_pmd counter.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces PMD-level swap entries for anonymous THPs, allowing huge mappings to survive the swap round-trip and reducing page-table overhead. When a PMD-mapped anonymous THP is swapped out, it is split into PTE-level swap entries. The new PMD swap entry is a compact page-table encoding that can be restored directly on swap-in without waiting for khugepaged to collapse the range later. This approach reduces major faults and swap I/O rate, resulting in improved performance. The patch series is ordered so that every consumer can handle PMD swap entries before the swap-out producer starts installing them.

review_comments.author: Usama Arif (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the handling of PMD-mapped anonymous THPs on s390 architecture, where swap PMDs are not just fake PTE swap entries but have their own layout (RSTE). To accommodate this, the author added an exclusive bit to the RSTE swap layout and modified the common code to handle it. The patch includes changes to arch/s390/include/asm/pgtable.h.
review_comments.raw_body:
Prepare for keeping a PMD-mapped anonymous THP mapped by a PMD across the
swap round-trip, which makes PG_anon_exclusive have to survive in a swap
PMD and not just in a swap PTE.

s390 is the one architecture where a swap PMD is not a swap PTE in
disguise: it is an RSTE with its own layout, converted to a fake PTE swap
entry for the common code. Give it its own exclusive bit rather than
borrowing the PTE-format macro, and document it in the RSTE swap layout,
where bit 52 was listed as unused.

Cc: Alexander Gordeev <agordeev@linux.ibm.com>
Cc: Gerald Schaefer <gerald.schaefer@linux.ibm.com>

 1 file changed, 18 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)

diff --git a/arch/s390/include/asm/pgtable.h b/arch/s390/include/asm/pgtable.h
index 2d5c2ab06de98..afd886edf0594 100644
--- a/arch/s390/include/asm/pgtable.h
+++ b/arch/s390/include/asm/pgtable.h
@@ -333,6 +333,7 @@ void setup_protection_map(void);
 /* Common bits in region and segment table entries, for swap entries */
 #define _RST_ENTRY_COMM		0x0010	/* Common-Region/Segment, marks swap entry */
 #define _RST_ENTRY_INVALID	0x0020	/* invalid region/segment table entry */
+#define _RST_ENTRY_SWP_EXCLUSIVE 0x0800	/* SW exclusive swap bit, see mk_swap_rste() */
 
 #define _CRST_ENTRIES	2048	/* number of region/segment table entries */
 #define _PAGE_ENTRIES	256	/* number of page table entries	*/
@@ -893,6 +894,21 @@ static inline pmd_t pmd_clear_soft_dirty(pmd_t pmd)
 }
 
 #ifdef CONFIG_ARCH_HAS_PMD_SOFTLEAVES
+static inline pmd_t pmd_swp_mkexclusive(pmd_t pmd)
+{
+	return set_pmd_bit(pmd, __pgprot(_RST_ENTRY_SWP_EXCLUSIVE));
+}
+
+static inline bool pmd_swp_exclusive(pmd_t pmd)
+{
+	return pmd_val(pmd) & _RST_ENTRY_SWP_EXCLUSIVE;
+}
+
+static inline pmd_t pmd_swp_clear_exclusive(pmd_t pmd)
+{
+	return clear_pmd_bit(pmd, __pgprot(_RST_ENTRY_SWP_EXCLUSIVE));
+}
+
 #define pmd_swp_soft_dirty(pmd)		pmd_soft_dirty(pmd)
 #define pmd_swp_mksoft_dirty(pmd)	pmd_mksoft_dirty(pmd)
 #define pmd_swp_clear_soft_dirty(pmd)	pmd_clear_soft_dirty(pmd)
@@ -1900,15 +1916,15 @@ static inline swp_entry_t __swp_entry(unsigned long type, unsigned long offset)
  * Bits 59 and 63 are used to indicate the swap entry. Bit 58 marks the rste
  * as invalid.
  * A swap entry is indicated by bit pattern (rste & 0x011) == 0x010
- * |			  offset			|Xtype |11TT|S0|
+ * |			  offset			|Etype |11TT|S0|
  * |0000000000111111111122222222223333333333444444444455|555555|5566|66|
  * |0123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901|234567|8901|23|
  *
  * Bits 0-51 store the offset.
+ * Bit 52 (E) is used to remember PG_anon_exclusive (_RST_ENTRY_SWP_EXCLUSIVE).
  * Bits 53-57 store the type.
  * Bit 62 (S) is used for softdirty tracking.
  * Bits 60-61 (TT) indicate the table type: 0x01 for REGION3 and 0x00 for SEGMENT.
- * Bit 52 (X) is unused.
  */
 
 #define __SWP_OFFSET_MASK_RSTE	((1UL << 52) - 1)

Prepare for keeping a PMD-mapped anonymous THP mapped by a PMD across the
swap round-trip, which makes PG_anon_exclusive have to survive in a swap
PMD and not just in a swap PTE.

x86-64 encodes a swap PMD exactly like a swap PTE, so the new helpers reuse
_PAGE_SWP_EXCLUSIVE, bit 3, which the swap-entry layout already reserves
for PG_anon_exclusive. 32-bit x86 aliases that bit to _PAGE_PSE and does
not select ARCH_HAS_PMD_SOFTLEAVES; assert that, because an exclusive swap
PMD would otherwise be pmd_present().

version_history.subject: [PATCH] rhashtable: specialize default comparison for constant parameters

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the default comparison function in the Linux kernel's rhashtable module by utilizing compile-time constants when possible, reducing the need for dynamic memory access and improving performance. The patch achieves this by passing constant parameters from the caller to the comparison function, allowing it to use scalar comparisons instead of the generic memcmp() function. This change is expected to improve performance in various areas of the kernel, including scheduling, networking, and file systems.

review_comments.summary:
Author addressed David's concern that the inline helpers and rhashtable_compare function should compare the same bytes, explaining that they do so by using a ?: operator to select between constant parameters and ht->p in case of dynamic parameter blocks.

Author addressed David Laight's concern that the patch relies on a pointer comparison for ht->p, explaining that it's a copy embedded in struct rhashtable and not a pointer, thus eliminating the need for a runtime branch.
review_comments.raw_body:

Thanks for taking a look!

They mustn't differ: the inline helpers take the same params that were
passed to rhashtable_init(). The only exception is a constant key_len of
0, which means the length is only known at init time (the BPF resizable
hashmap does this). That's why the constant arm has "?: ht->p.key_len".

compiler which copy to read. rht_key_get_hash() has done the same since
de91b25c8011 from Herbert.

ht->p is a copy embedded in struct rhashtable, not a pointer, so there's
no address to compare. __builtin_constant_p() is resolved at compile
time, so there's no runtime branch either.
